analysis.one_liner: Sets water pollution limits for PFAS chemicals and funds treatment plants to comply.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee with 13 Democratic-aligned cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the EPA to set deadlines for two things under the Clean Water Act: water quality limits telling states how much PFAS — the 'forever chemicals' found in nonstick pans, waterproof clothing, and firefighting foam — can be in water before it threatens human health, and discharge limits for nine specific industries that pipe PFAS into waterways, such as plastics makers, paper mills, and textile plants. It also authorized $200 million a year through 2026 in grants to publicly owned sewage treatment plants to help them remove the chemicals. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water, fish, or live downstream from industrial dischargers — effectively everyone exposed to PFAS, which is most Americans. PFAS have been linked to health harms and are extremely persistent, so limiting discharges reduces ongoing contamination. Communities served by public wastewater plants also benefit from federal grants covering the cost of new treatment technology.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS chemical and class within two years of enactment, establishing how much PFAS in water is likely to harm health.

Requires EPA to publish a final rule within four years setting effluent limitations — legal caps on what industries can pipe into public waters, including into sewage plants — for nine priority industries: organic chemicals and plastics, pulp and paper, textile mills, electroplating, metal finishing, leather tanning, paint formulating, electrical and electronic components, and plastics molding.

Authorizes $200 million per year for fiscal years 2022 through 2026 in grants to publicly owned treatment works to implement the new discharge limits, so the cost of cleaning wastewater does not fall entirely on local ratepayers.

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge PFAS-bearing wastewater — chemical manufacturers, plastics and synthetic fibers plants, paper mills, textile mills, metal finishers, and electronics makers — would bear compliance costs, some of which would likely pass through to consumers in the form of higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial PFAS dischargers, and consumers indirectly

drawbacks.text: The $200 million annual grants are an authorization, not an appropriation — Congress would still have to vote the money each year, and the bill specifies no funding source.
Compliance with new effluent limits would cost covered industries money, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices for goods like paper, textiles, and electronics.
The bill addresses only point-source discharges — PFAS leaving a pipe, including into sewage plants — so it would not directly clean up PFAS already in soil, groundwater, or contaminated sites.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit — hard, enforceable deadlines for limits on chemicals linked to health harms and already present in most Americans' blood and drinking water — outweighs the compliance costs, which are spread across the industries that create the contamination rather than only on downstream communities. The grants soften the burden on municipal ratepayers. The main design limits are that it covers pipe discharges only and its money depends on future appropriations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on May 27, 2021, read twice, and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it stayed until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on May 27, 2021, joined on the original text by eight Senate Democrats including Schumer, Warren, Durbin, and Feinstein.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill: 11 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Independents; no Republican cosponsor signed on.
The action history records no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor consideration — before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries that discharge PFAS into waterways — chemical manufacturers, plastics makers, paper mills, and textile plants — are better off because the bill never became law; they face no new enforceable discharge limits or compliance costs. The EPA also faces no court-enforceable statutory deadlines for setting PFAS water criteria.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; all 13 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and none of the 50 Republicans signed on, so support was entirely Democratic-leaning, but no floor vote shows how the chamber as a whole would have split.

industries.note: Companies that make PFAS and the organic chemicals, plastics, and synthetic fibers category named in the bill would face discharge limits for their products' wastewater, including discharges into municipal sewage plants. The bill's failure means no new enforceable caps on those discharges.

Named as a priority industry that would have had to meet PFAS effluent limits within four years. Consumers of PFAS-treated food packaging and paper products could see some of those costs passed through.

Named as a priority industry for PFAS discharge limits; waterproof and stain-resistant fabric production relies heavily on PFAS. The bill's failure leaves their discharges unregulated by these standards.

industries.note: Three named priority industries that would face PFAS effluent limits. Failure of the bill avoids their compliance costs.

The bill authorized $200 million a year through 2026 to help municipal treatment works implement new PFAS discharge limits, protecting local ratepayers from bearing the full cost. With the bill dead, the plants get no federal money and stay exposed to PFAS arriving from industrial customers.
